en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Food, 36.
The Second Training Rule on Invitation.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, two monks were traveling along the highway toward Sāvatthī in the Kosala country.
One monk engaged in improper conduct.
The second monk said this to that monk:
“Friend, do not do such a thing; this is not allowable.
He became resentful toward him.
Then those bhikkhus went to Sāvatthī.
Now at that time, a certain guild in Sāvatthī had prepared a meal for the Saṅgha.
A second monk had already finished eating and was invited to abstain from further food.
Another monk, being resentful, went to a family of his relatives, took almsfood, and approached that first monk; having approached him, he said this to that monk:
“Eat, friend,” he said.
“Enough, friend; I am full,” he replied.
“The alms-food is excellent, friend; eat it,” he said.
Then that bhikkhu, being pressured by the other bhikkhu, ate that almsfood.
Being resentful, the bhikkhu said this to him:
"Friend, you too think you ought to be spoken to when you eat food that is not left over, even though you have already finished eating and been invited to stop."
“Surely, friend, it should be explained.
“Surely, friend, it should be asked.
Then that bhikkhu reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
Those monks who were few in desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can a monk invite a monk who has already finished his meal and refused further food to eat with food that is not left over?"... [and so on]...
"Is it true, monk, that you invited a monk who had already finished his meal and refused further food to eat with food that was not left over?"
“It is true, Blessed One,” he replied.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, invite a monk who has already finished his meal and refused further food to accept food that is not left over?”
“Monk, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
‘Whatever monk, to a monk who has already finished his meal and refused further food, should offer fresh or soft food that is not left over...’”
Or if one should offer it or invite [the other] to eat, saying, ‘Come, monk, eat or consume,’ and knowing [it is so], with the intent to offend, when the other has eaten,
there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whoever,” however—
Whoever is such a one … [as described] … “a bhikkhu” … [and so on] … this is the meaning intended here by the term “bhikkhu.”
"A bhikkhunī" means another bhikkhu.
"One who has eaten" (bhuttāvī) means:
Any one of the five kinds of cooked food has been eaten, even if only as much as the tip of a blade of kusa grass.
"Invited" means that the meal is manifest, the food is manifest, [the donor] offers it while standing within arm's reach, and a refusal is manifest.
What is called "not left over" (anatiritta) is that which has been made unallowable (akappiyakata) and that which has been made unaccepted (appaṭiggahitakata).
It is done when [the food] has not been announced;
it is done outside the range of hand-reach;
it is done by one who has not yet eaten.
It has been done by one who has finished eating, who has refused further food, and who has risen from his seat;
it has not been said, "Enough, this is all";
and it is not the remainder of what was left over by one who is not ill.
This is what is called "not left over.
As for "hard food":
with the exception of the five kinds of cooked food, that which is for a watch of the night, that which is for seven days, and that which is for life—all the remainder is called "hard food."
"Edible food" means the five kinds of cooked food: boiled rice, sour gruel, flour cakes, fish, and meat.
"Should invite him to accept" means...
"Take as much as you wish.
"He knows" means either he knows by himself, or others inform him, or he informs [them] himself.
“With the intention of finding fault”:

thinking, “By means of this, I will accuse him, remind him, counter-accuse him, cause him to be reminded, or make him feel dejected,” one brings it forward; there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
By his word, [thinking] “I will eat, I will consume,” one accepts it; there is an offense of wrong-doing.
For every mouthful, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
At the conclusion of the meal, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If one who has already been invited, perceiving that he has been invited, offers hard food or soft food that is not left over, there is an offense entailing expiation.
If one who has already invited [another] is doubtful, yet invites them by bringing food—whether soft food or hard food—that is not leftover, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one who has already invited another perceives that they have not been invited, yet invites them by bringing food—whether soft food or hard food—that is not leftover, there is no offense.
If one brings for the purpose of food anything that is to be consumed at the proper time, for seven days, or for as long as life lasts, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If, at his word, one accepts [the food] thinking, "I will eat it, I will consume it," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one has not been invited to eat, yet perceives that one has been invited, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If he has not been invited and he is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If he has not been invited and he perceives that he has not been invited, there is no offense.
There is no offense—
He gives it after having it made into leftover food;
he gives it saying, "Eat it after having it made into leftover food";
or he gives it saying, "Go, taking this for the sake of another."
He gives the remainder to one who is ill;
he gives it saying, "Use this—whether it be for a watch of the night, for seven days, or for as long as life lasts—provided there is a suitable occasion";
or [he gives it] to one who is insane.
"For one who is a first offender.
The sixth training rule on the second invitation ceremony is finished.
